chunks: How to select a buck converter IC. The question: How do you select a buck converter IC?
Choosing a buck IC means writing down what your circuit needs, then checking each candidate against those numbers.
Start with the input voltage range, the output voltage, and the load current.
Then check that the chip can handle the duty cycle, stay cool, and meet any needs for battery life, noise, and size.
It is like choosing a truck for a job. You first ask how heavy the load is (current), how rough the road is (input voltage spikes), and how far you drive (heat and efficiency).
You never buy the biggest truck, but you want some margin. A truck that barely fits the load will wear out fast.
The analogy skips one buck-specific limit: the switch cannot turn on for less than a minimum time.
On-time shrinks as 1 over f SW and is shortest at maximum input.
At 2 megahertz and 18 volts it drops below an assumed 100 nanoseconds minimum on-time, so the part would skip pulses. At 500 kilohertz there is plenty of room.
The 100 nanoseconds line is illustrative; real minimum on-times vary by part.
Input range: the lowest and highest voltage the supply may reach, including spikes. Duty cycle (D): the fraction of each period the switch is on, about V out over V in .
Minimum on-time: the shortest pulse the chip can make. Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon, which must stay under its limit.
Quiescent current: the current the chip burns just to stay alive.
Say you need 3. 3 volts at 2 amps from a 12 volts supply, switching at 500 kilohertz. The duty cycle is 3. 3 over 12 equals 0.
275 and the period is 2 microseconds, so each on-pulse lasts about 0. 55 microseconds. That is longer than a typical minimum on-time of around 100 nanoseconds, so it is fine.
If you plug in a live 12 volts cable, the voltage can briefly ring (overshoot and bounce) up to about 24 volts, so you want a part rated for 28 volts or more.
You also want a current rating above 2 amps, such as 3 amps. That is the whole idea.
"I start with requirements: input range including transients, output voltage and current, ripple, efficiency, size, quiescent current.
Then I filter by input voltage with margin, current rating and current limit, and check the duty cycle against the IC's minimum on-time at my chosen frequency.
I estimate losses and junction temperature, then look at control mode, light-load behaviour, protections, package and cost.
I'd shortlist two or three parts, compare on a spreadsheet, and validate on the bench."
